_comment: Lesson metadata strings for Speed Math Learn section. English locale.

add_in_parts.title: Addition
add_in_parts.why_it_works: Breaking a number into tens and ones lets you do two simple additions instead of one hard one.
add_in_parts.common_mistake: Forgetting to add the ones part after adding the tens.

subtract_in_parts.title: Subtraction
subtract_in_parts.why_it_works: Left-to-right subtraction processes place values directly without scratchpad borrowing, solving deficits cleanly.
subtract_in_parts.common_mistake: Borrowing right-to-left mentally instead of taking the whole tens/hundreds difference and adjusting.

multiplication_hub.title: Multiplication
multiplication_hub.why_it_works: The Vertically & Crosswise (Criss-Cross) method calculates units, cross-products, and higher places directly in a single line, eliminating multi-line scratchpad additions.
multiplication_hub.common_mistake: Forgetting to add the carry from the previous step to the cross-product sum.

division_hub.title: Division
division_hub.why_it_works: Divisibility rules and multiplicative inversion convert difficult multi-digit divisions into fast mental multiplication and single-digit checks.
division_hub.common_mistake: Dividing by composite divisors directly without factoring them into single-digit chunks.

multiply_2x2.title: 2-Digit Multiplication
multiply_2x2.why_it_works: The Vertically & Crosswise (Criss-Cross) method calculates units, cross-products, and tens directly into a single line, eliminating multi-line scratchpad additions.
multiply_2x2.common_mistake: Forgetting to add the carry from the previous step to the cross-product sum.

multiply_3x2.title: 3×2 Digit Multiplication
multiply_3x2.why_it_works: Expanding the crosswise pattern to 4 stages allows multiplying any 3-digit by 2-digit number in a single row without zero-padding scratch lines.
multiply_3x2.common_mistake: Mixing up the inner vertical digit and the outer diagonal digit during the hundreds step.

multiply_3x3.title: 3-Digit Multiplication
multiply_3x3.why_it_works: The 5-step star crosswise algorithm (1 → 2 → 3 → 2 → 1) computes 3-digit products directly by place values, holding carries in memory.
multiply_3x3.common_mistake: Leaving out the middle vertical product in the 3-way star step.

divide_by_5_25.title: Divide by 5, 25 & 125
divide_by_5_25.why_it_works: 5 = 10÷2, 25 = 100÷4, and 125 = 1000÷8. Inverting to multiplication by 2, 4, or 8 and shifting the decimal point is instant mentally.
divide_by_5_25.common_mistake: Shifting the decimal point the wrong number of places or in the wrong direction.

divide_by_9_99.title: Division by 9 & 99
divide_by_9_99.why_it_works: When dividing by 9, the quotient digits are simply the running sums of the dividend digits.
divide_by_9_99.common_mistake: Forgetting that the last running sum is the remainder, not part of the quotient.

factor_division.title: Factor Division
factor_division.why_it_works: Decomposing a composite 2-digit divisor into single-digit factors allows fast sequential division.
factor_division.common_mistake: Dividing by factors that do not multiply to the original divisor.

reciprocal_division.title: Reciprocal & Decimals
reciprocal_division.why_it_works: Dividing by decimals like 0.5, 0.25, and 2.5 is equivalent to multiplying by their whole number reciprocals 2, 4, and 0.4.
reciprocal_division.common_mistake: Confusing dividing by 0.5 (which doubles) with dividing by 2 (which halves).

flag_division.title: Straight Division
flag_division.why_it_works: The Dhvajanka (Flag) method breaks divisors into a 1-digit Base and a Flag digit for single-line straight division.
flag_division.common_mistake: Forgetting to subtract the Flag adjustment from the working dividend.

multiply_by_5_25.title: Multiply by 5, 25 & 125
multiply_by_5_25.why_it_works: 5 = 10÷2, 25 = 100÷4, 75 = 100−25, and 125 = 1000÷8. Dividing then multiplying by round powers of 10 is much faster.
multiply_by_5_25.common_mistake: Forgetting to multiply by 10, 100 or 1000 after dividing.

multiply_by_11.title: Multiply by 11
multiply_by_11.why_it_works: 11 × n = 10n + n. The middle digit is the sum of the two outer digits.
multiply_by_11.common_mistake: Forgetting to carry when the digit sum is 10 or more.

multiply_by_99.title: Multiply by 9, 99 & 999
multiply_by_99.why_it_works: n × (10^k − 1) = n × 10^k − n. Multiplying by 10, 100, or 1000 is instant; then subtract n.
multiply_by_99.common_mistake: Subtracting 1 instead of subtracting the original number n.

near_100_mult.title: Near-100 Multiplication
near_100_mult.why_it_works: Both numbers are near 100, so their gaps are small and easy to multiply.
near_100_mult.common_mistake: Forgetting to zero-pad the right part when the gap product is less than 10.

squares_ending_5.title: Squares Ending in 5
squares_ending_5.why_it_works: Any number ending in 5 squares to 100×k(k+1)+25 — always ending in 25!
squares_ending_5.common_mistake: Using the wrong leading digit — use the part before the 5.

split_percentages.title: Split Percentages
split_percentages.why_it_works: Any percentage can be split into 10%, 5%, and 1% chunks — all easy to compute.
split_percentages.common_mistake: Adding parts incorrectly, or miscounting how many 10% chunks fit.

fraction_pct_friends.title: Fraction to Percentage
fraction_pct_friends.why_it_works: Knowing key fraction ↔ % pairs by heart cuts computation time to zero.

percentage_to_fraction.title: Percentage to Fraction
percentage_to_fraction.why_it_works: Replacing decimal percentages with simplest fractions turns complex multiplications into instant single-digit divisions.
percentage_to_fraction.common_mistake: Forgetting the base unit family (e.g. confusing 37.5% from 1/8 with 1/6 or 1/7).
